env.name: PORT
env.why: The only variable this app reads. A search of src/ for process.env, config-file reads and settings modules returns exactly one hit: src/server.js:15, `var port = process.env.PORT || 3000`. That port is the whole of the app's own origin — there is no base URL setting, no callback URL, no CORS allowlist and no feature flag anywhere in src/. 3000 is set explicitly rather than left to the `|| 3000` default so that app_url, the runbook and the port the process actually binds cannot drift apart. The test suite is unaffected by it: tests/helpers.js binds port 0 and lets the OS choose, and the one test that runs src/server.js as a child process asks the OS for a free port and overrides PORT for that child, so `npm test` passes with PORT=3000 set and the app already holding 3000 — checked here, both ways round.

dropped.why: Linting is the static gate's job: `bsf gates static` runs the repo's own linter and compares each rule's per-file count against .factory/guardrails/baselines.json. Putting it in `build`, `test` or `coverage` would turn a baselined violation into a build failure and would count the same finding twice. `npm run lint` still reports 36 violations (no-var 32, eqeqeq 3, no-console 1) on untouched code, so a build that included it would fail every time. It is still runnable in the sandbox once `npm ci` has run; it is just not in the build path. Re-checked this round now that tests/ exists: eslint.config.mjs scopes its one config block to `files: ["src/**/*.js"]`, so the six new files under tests/ match no config and are linted by no rule — `npx eslint .` and `npx eslint src` both report the same 36. The baselines in .factory/guardrails/baselines.json are therefore still exact, and adding tests did not move the static gate.

dropped.what: a `coverage` npm script, as the thing commands.coverage calls
dropped.why: commands.coverage spells the node invocation out in full instead of adding `"coverage": "..."` to package.json. Setup writes nothing into the repo that is kept, so a script added here would not exist when the gate runs, and this amendment is explicitly not allowed to ship a repo patch. The spelled-out form also keeps the relationship to commands.test visible: both are `node --test` with the same default file discovery over tests/*.test.js, so they run the same 52 tests, and the extra flags only add coverage instrumentation and a second reporter. If someone later adds an `npm run coverage` script, this field should become `npm run coverage` through a further amendment rather than the two drifting apart.

dropped.what: the default whole-process coverage scope, and the `--test-coverage-lines`/`--test-coverage-branches` thresholds
dropped.why: `--test-coverage-include='src/**'` narrows the report to the app's own five files. Without it node also reports on tests/helpers.js and on whatever the runner injects through NODE_OPTIONS — on this machine a `node-trust.cjs` shim from outside the repo, which alone dragged the reported total from 98.04% to 81.14%. Narrowing is safe for the gate: bsf's diff-coverage skips any changed file that is absent from the report (`if (entry === undefined) continue`), so a PR that only touches tests/ measures as nothing-to-measure rather than as uncovered. The threshold flags are left off deliberately — the floor lives in .factory/guardrails/coverage.json and the runner ratchets it; a second threshold inside the command would fail the run before the gate ever read the number.

Replaced with `npm ci`, which installs exactly what the committed package-lock.json pins and fails loudly if the lock file and package.json disagree, so the sandbox cannot silently resolve a different dependency tree from one round to the next. `npm ci` is the command actually run and verified here; `npm install` was not. Re-verified this round after the tests landed: the lock file is unchanged, 159 packages, exit 0 — node's test runner is built in, so the repo's first test suite added no dependency.

Replaced with the equivalent `node src/server.js` — `start` runs that same file. The trial stops the app by signalling the process group, and running node directly means there is no npm wrapper process between the signal and the server. `npm start` stays in the runbook as the command a developer would type.

not_exercised.what: The four lines of src/server.js that only run when the file is the entry point
not_exercised.why: src/server.js:18-21 is the body of the `if (require.main === module)` guard — the app.listen call and its `listening on` log. Every in-process test imports the module instead of being it, so those lines never execute inside the coverage run and server.js reports 82.61% of lines rather than 100%. They are not untested: tests/server.test.js spawns `node src/server.js` as a child with PORT set, waits for the `listening on <port>` line and fetches /health through it. Node's coverage only instruments the process it runs in, so the child's execution is invisible to the report. Treat 82.61% on that file as the ceiling for in-process coverage, not as a gap to close by deleting the guard — fundamentals.md records the guard as the deliberate testing seam.

not_exercised.what: Anything that has to survive a restart
not_exercised.why: The store is two module-level variables in src/db.js (`items` and `nextId`). Every restart empties the table and resets ids to 1, and nothing is written to disk. The tests work around it rather than solving it: tests/helpers.js has a `reset()` that removes every item through db.remove, and tests/db.test.js asserts outright that ids keep climbing after a remove and are not reused — so a test must use the id add() hands back, never a literal 1. A change about durability, a schema, a migration or a move to a real database still cannot be verified here; it would need a database service added by an amendment episode.

One node process holding state in its own heap: no cluster mode, no worker pool, no lock, no transaction. Two requests interleaving inside db.add or db.remove cannot be reproduced, and nothing about state shared across processes can be checked. The tests do not change this — they run in-process against the same module state, which is why helpers.reset() exists. require-atomic-updates is installed as a guardrail precisely because this class of bug has no runtime check here.

not_exercised.what: HTTPS, a reverse proxy, a non-localhost origin, or any deployment concern
not_exercised.why: The app listens on plain HTTP and the sandbox reaches it at 127.0.0.1:3000. The repo has no Dockerfile, compose file, devcontainer or deploy configuration, so nothing here describes another origin. Secure cookie flags, `trust proxy`, CORS, HSTS and host-based routing have no environment in this sandbox to be checked against.

express is the single runtime dependency and src/ makes no outbound network call of any kind, so there is nothing to stub and no provider test mode to name. The stubs list is empty because none is needed, not because one was skipped. A change that adds an outbound call needs an amendment episode to add its stub before it can be verified.

not_exercised.what: Authentication, authorization and anything behind a sign-in
not_exercised.why: There is nothing behind a sign-in to reach: no users, no sessions, no cookies, no identity provider and no authorization check anywhere in src/. Every one of the six routes is public and anonymous, and all six were exercised. This is a statement that the feature does not exist, not that an identity provider was left unstubbed.

not_exercised.what: Static analysis of the test suite itself
not_exercised.why: eslint.config.mjs contains one config block, scoped to `files: ["src/**/*.js"]`. The six files under tests/ match no block, so eslint applies no rule to them: `npx eslint .` reports the same 36 violations as `npx eslint src`. The tests use `var` throughout and would carry roughly as many no-var findings as src/ if they were in scope. That is not a sandbox limitation — it is a guardrail-scope decision, and an amendment is not allowed to change guardrails. Widening the config to tests/ is a setup or gardening change, and whoever makes it should expect the static gate to record a fresh per-file baseline for tests/ on the same commit.

not_exercised.what: The `env -i` closed-environment form of the install
not_exercised.why: Running `npm ci` under `env -i` with only PATH, HOME, TMPDIR, LANG, CI and PORT failed here with EAI_AGAIN on registry.npmjs.org, because stripping the environment also strips this runner's proxy configuration. The same `npm ci` with the environment intact succeeded. So what is verified is that the install needs nothing of a developer's own environment beyond reaching the registry; what is not verified is that it works with the proxy settings removed. registry.npmjs.org is listed under egress for that reason. Note that `npm test` and `commands.coverage` have no such caveat: both were run under exactly that stripped environment and passed, because neither touches the network.
